hello.title: Hello, Lisp
hello.summary: Write your first Lisp program, print text with format and calculate with prefix notation.
hello.lesson.0: Common Lisp is one of the oldest programming languages that people still use today. A Lisp program is a series of **forms**. A form in parentheses is a call: the first element names the operator, and the other elements are its arguments. This program prints one line:
hello.lesson.2: `format` prints text. Its first argument is the destination: `t` means the screen (the standard output). The second argument is the text in double quotes, called a **string**. Inside it, `~%` starts a new line. A semicolon `;` starts a comment, which Lisp ignores until the end of the line.
hello.lesson.5: In Lisp, the operator always comes first: you write `(+ 2 3)` instead of `2 + 3`. This is called **prefix notation**. A form like this, with parentheses around it, is also called an **s-expression** (symbolic expression). `+` and `*` accept any number of arguments, and `-` and `/` work the same way.
hello.lesson.6: To print a value, put `~a` into the string. `format` replaces each `~a` with the next argument after the string. Forms can be nested: Lisp evaluates the inner form first, so `(* 2 (+ 3 4))` becomes `(* 2 7)` and then `14`.
hello.lesson.9: `~s` also inserts a value, but it shows it the way Lisp reads it, so a string keeps its double quotes. The function `print` shows a value in the same way. It writes a new line first, then the value, then a space. That is why this course mostly uses `format` for clean output.
hello.lesson.11: Every opening parenthesis needs a closing one. Most Lisp editors show you which parentheses belong together, and programmers read Lisp code by its indentation.
hello.card.0: `(format t "Hi~%")` prints `Hi` and a new line
hello.card.1: `~a` inserts the next argument, `~s` keeps quotes
hello.card.4: `(print x)` new line, value with quotes, space
hello-1.explain: `(+ 4 5)` adds 4 and 5, and `~a` puts the result into the text.
hello-2.explain: The inner form `(+ 1 4)` is 5. Then `(* 2 5)` is 10.
hello-3.explain: In Lisp the operator always comes first, inside the parentheses.
hello-4.explain: The first string has no `~%`, so no new line follows `Hi`. The second text continues on the same line.
hello-5.statement: Inside a `format` string, `~%` starts a new line.
hello-5.explain: `~%` is the directive for a new line. Without it, the next output continues on the same line.
hello-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Sum: 7`.
hello-6.explain: `~a` is replaced by the next argument, the result of `(+ 3 4)`.
hello-7.prompt: Build a form that prints the result of 10 minus 4.
hello-7.explain: The operator `-` comes first, then 10 and 4. `format` prints the result with `~a`.
hello-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Hello, Lisp!` and then `2`.
hello-8.explain: The forms run from top to bottom. `Hello, ` has no new line, so `Lisp!` follows on the same line.
hello-9.explain: Lisp uses prefix notation. Write `(* 3 4)` instead of `(3 * 4)`.

hello-11.options.1: On the same line, without quotes

hello-11.explain: `print` writes a new line first and shows strings the way Lisp reads them, with quotes.
hello-12.explain: The first `~a` gets `(- 10 3)`, which is 7. The second gets `(/ 8 2)`, which is 4.
values.title: Values
values.summary: Work with numbers, exact ratios, strings, symbols, t and nil, and name values with defparameter.
values.lesson.0: Lisp has whole numbers (integers) like `42` and decimal numbers (floats) like `2.5`. Integers can be as large as you need. `expt` raises a number to a power, so `(expt 2 100)` is 2 to the power of 100.
values.lesson.2: When you divide two integers and the result is not whole, Lisp gives an exact fraction called a **ratio**: `(/ 10 4)` is `5/2`. If one number is a float, the result is a float. `mod` gives the remainder of a division: `(mod 17 5)` is `2`.
values.lesson.5: A string is text in double quotes. `length` counts its characters, and `string-upcase` returns it in capital letters. `(concatenate 'string "a" "b")` joins strings into one new string.
values.lesson.6: A **symbol** is a name. The quote `'` tells Lisp: do not evaluate this, take it as it is. So `'apple` is the symbol `APPLE`. Lisp turns symbol names into capital letters when it reads them, so they print in capitals. In `concatenate`, the symbol `'string` says what kind of result you want.
values.lesson.9: Lisp writes true as `t` and false as `nil`. Comparisons return one of them: `>` (greater than), `<` (less than), `>=`, `<=` and `=` (equal numbers). `(< 1 2 3)` checks that each number is smaller than the next. Functions that answer a yes or no question often end in `p`, like `stringp` (is it a string?). Every value except `nil` counts as true.
values.lesson.11: `(defparameter *price* 12)` creates a global variable named `*price*` with the value `12`. The stars around the name are a convention for global variables. Names can contain hyphens, like `*max-speed*`.
values.lesson.13: Because Lisp turns names into capital letters, `*Price*` and `*price*` are the same variable. Most Lisp programmers write all code in lowercase.
values-1.explain: 12 divided by 8 is not whole, so Lisp gives the exact ratio `3/2`.
values-2.explain: 6 fits into 20 three times (18), and the remainder is 2.
values-3.explain: The quote makes `hello` a symbol. Lisp stores symbol names in capital letters.
values-4.prompt: Which value counts as false in Lisp?
values-4.explain: Only `nil` is false. Every other value, even `0` and the empty string, counts as true.
values-5.explain: Both numbers are integers, so the result is the exact ratio `5/2`. Write `(/ 10 4.0)` to get `2.5`.
values-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `2.5`.
values-6.explain: With the float `2.0`, the result is a float: `2.5`. With `2` the result is the ratio `5/2`.
values-7.prompt: Build a line that creates a global variable `*speed*` with the value 50.
values-7.explain: `defparameter` takes the name and then the value.
values-8.explain: The variable is called `*height*`, with stars. `height` without stars does not exist.
values-9.prompt: Match the value with its kind.
values-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `10 and 15`.
values-10.explain: `*b*` uses `*a*`, so `*a*` must exist first. The program prints both values at the end.
values-11.explain: `<` checks that each number is smaller than the next. 5 is not smaller than 3, so the result is `NIL`.
values-12.explain: `concatenate` joins the strings into `abcde`, which has 5 characters.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Define your own functions with defun, use parameters and return values, and write functions without a name.
functions.lesson.0: `defun` defines a function. After `defun` comes the name, then a list of **parameters** in parentheses, then the body. A function returns the value of the last form in its body. Lisp needs no `return` keyword.
functions.lesson.2: A function can have several parameters. You call your own functions like the built-in ones: the name first, then the arguments.
functions.lesson.4: The body can contain several forms. Lisp runs them in order, but only the value of the last one is returned. Here the function prints a greeting and returns the length of the name.
functions.lesson.6: Functions can call other functions. A function without parameters has an empty list `()`.
functions.lesson.9: `(lambda (x) (* x 10))` creates a function without a name. It has a parameter list and a body, like `defun`. You can call it directly by putting it first in a form. In the unit about higher-order functions, you pass such functions to other functions.
functions.lesson.11: Lisp programmers write names in lowercase with hyphens between words, like `four-times` or `celsius-to-fahrenheit`.
functions.lesson.12: A call needs exactly as many arguments as the function has parameters. `(square 2 3)` stops the program with an error.
functions.card.0: `(defun name (a b) body)` defines a function
functions.card.1: The last form of the body is the return value
functions-1.explain: `triple` multiplies its argument by 3, and 3 times 7 is 21.
functions-2.explain: The arguments go into the parameters in order: `a` is 3 and `b` is 10, so the result is `(- 3 10)`.
functions-3.explain: Both forms run, but only the value of the last form, `(+ x 1)`, is returned.
functions-4.statement: A Lisp function needs a `return` statement to give back a value.
functions-4.explain: A function returns the value of the last form in its body automatically.

functions-5.explain: `defun` defines a named function. `lambda` creates a function without a name.

functions-6.explain: After `defun` comes the name and then the parameter list in parentheses.

functions-7.explain: The function must be defined before it is called. Then the calls print 8 and 27.

conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Let your program choose with if, when, unless and cond, and combine tests with and, or and not.
conditions.lesson.0: `(if test then else)` has three parts. When the test is true (anything except `nil`), Lisp evaluates the `then` form. Otherwise it evaluates the `else` form.
conditions.lesson.2: `if` returns a value, like every form in Lisp. You can use it inside other forms, for example as the body of a function.
conditions.lesson.4: `when` runs its body only when the test is true. `unless` runs its body only when the test is false. Both can contain several forms, but they have no `else` part. When the body does not run, they return `nil`.
conditions.lesson.7: `cond` checks several clauses in order. Each clause is a list: a test, then the result. Only the first clause whose test is true runs. A last clause with the test `t` is always true, so it catches all other cases.
conditions.lesson.10: `(and a b)` is true when all its arguments are true, and `(or a b)` when at least one is. `and` returns the last value, `or` returns the first value that is not `nil`. `(not x)` turns `nil` into `T` and every other value into `NIL`. `evenp` and `oddp` check whether a number is even or odd.
conditions.lesson.12: `=` compares only numbers. To compare strings, use `equal`: `(equal "yes" "yes")` is `T`.
conditions.card.0: `(if test then else)` returns a value
conditions.card.2: `(cond (test1 a) (test2 b) (t c))` first true clause
conditions-1.explain: 7 is not even, so `evenp` returns `nil` and the `else` form runs.
conditions-2.explain: 150 is neither below 10 nor below 100, so only the last clause with `t` matches.
conditions-3.explain: All values are true, so `and` returns the last one: `3`.
conditions-4.explain: 2 is not greater than 5. So `when` does not run its body, but `unless` does.
conditions-5.statement: In Lisp, the number `0` counts as false in an `if`.
conditions-5.explain: Only `nil` is false. `0` is a normal value, so it counts as true.
conditions-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `adult`.
conditions-6.explain: `if` chooses between two values. `when` has no else part: it would return the last form, `"child"`.
conditions-7.prompt: Build a test that is true when `n` is even and greater than 10.
conditions-7.explain: `and` is true only when both tests are true.
conditions-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `negative zero`.
conditions-8.explain: The function comes first. Inside `cond`, the clause with `t` must be the last one.
conditions-9.explain: `=` works only with numbers. Use `(equal lang "es")` to compare strings.

conditions-12.explain: `or` returns the first value that is not `nil`, which is 7.
lists.title: Lists
lists.summary: Build lists with list and cons, take them apart with first and rest, and join them with append.
lists.lesson.0: A list holds values in order. `(list 1 2 3)` creates a list. You can also write a list with a quote: `'(1 2 3)`. The quote stops Lisp from treating the list as a call. With `~a`, a list prints in parentheses.
lists.lesson.2: `first` returns the first element. `rest` returns a list of all the other elements. The older names `car` and `cdr` do the same, and you see them often in Lisp code. `(nth 2 list)` returns the element at position 2, counting from 0.
lists.lesson.5: `cons` puts a value in front of a list and returns the new list. Inside, a list is a chain of **cons cells**: each cell holds one value (the `car`) and the rest of the list (the `cdr`). The empty list is `nil`, which you can also write as `()`.
lists.lesson.8: `length` counts the elements. `append` joins lists into one, and `reverse` returns the elements in the opposite order. `null` checks whether a list is empty.
lists.lesson.10: `cons`, `append` and `reverse` do not change the original list. They return a new list.
lists.lesson.11: Without a quote, `(1 2 3)` is a call: Lisp tries to use `1` as a function and stops with an error. Write `'(1 2 3)` or `(list 1 2 3)`.
lists-1.explain: `rest` returns `(20 30)`, and its first element is 20.
lists-2.explain: `append` joins the three lists into `(1 2 3 4 5)`, which has 5 elements.
lists-3.explain: `cons` puts the symbol `A` in front of the list `(B C)`.
lists-4.explain: The list has only one element, so the rest is the empty list, `NIL`.
lists-5.explain: `car` is the old name of `first`. Both return the first element of a list.
lists-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `(8 15)`.
lists-6.explain: `rest` returns all elements except the first one.
lists-7.prompt: Build a form that puts 0 in front of the list `(1 2)`.
lists-7.explain: `cons` takes the new element first and the list second.

lists-10.pairs.2: A new list with 1 in front

mapping.title: Higher-order functions
mapping.summary: Pass functions to other functions: transform lists with mapcar, filter with remove-if-not and combine with reduce.
mapping.lesson.0: In Lisp, functions are values. `#'square` means the function named `square`; it is short for `(function square)`. A function that takes other functions as arguments is called a **higher-order function**.
mapping.lesson.1: `mapcar` calls a function on every element of a list and returns a new list with the results.
mapping.lesson.3: Often you pass a `lambda` instead of a named function. With two lists, `mapcar` takes one element from each list for every call.
mapping.lesson.6: `remove-if-not` keeps only the elements for which the test function returns true. `remove-if` does the opposite: it removes them.
mapping.lesson.9: `reduce` combines all elements into one value with a function of two arguments. `(reduce #'+ '(1 2 3 4))` first adds 1 and 2, then adds 3 to the result, then 4. `max` returns the largest of its arguments.
mapping.lesson.11: `funcall` calls a function that you have as a value, for example in a parameter. With it, you can write your own higher-order functions. `1+` adds one to a number.
mapping.lesson.13: Lisp keeps the names of functions and variables apart. That is why you need `#'` to pass a function, and `funcall` to call a function stored in a variable.
mapping.card.1: `(mapcar f list)` applies `f` to every element
mapping.card.4: `(funcall f x)` calls a function value
mapping-1.explain: `mapcar` doubles each element and returns the new list.
mapping-3.explain: `remove-if-not` keeps the elements for which `oddp` is true.
mapping-4.explain: `mapcar` collects the result of `evenp` for each element. It does not filter.
mapping-5.explain: `mapcar` returns a new list. The original list stays the same.

loops.title: Iteration and recursion
loops.summary: Repeat code with dotimes, dolist and loop, and solve problems with functions that call themselves.
loops.lesson.0: `(dotimes (i 3) body)` runs the body 3 times. The variable `i` counts from `0` up to, but not including, `3`.
loops.lesson.2: `(dolist (x list) body)` runs the body once for every element of a list. Each time, `x` holds the next element.
loops.lesson.5: `loop` is a small language of its own. `for i from 1 to 5` counts from 1 to 5, including both ends, and `for i below 3` counts from 0 to 2. `for x in list` goes through a list. `collect` builds a list of values, `sum` adds them up, and `do` runs forms. `downto` counts down.
loops.lesson.8: A **recursive** function calls itself. It needs a **base case**, a simple case that it answers without calling itself. The factorial of `n` is `n` times the factorial of `n - 1`, and the factorial of 1 is 1.
loops.lesson.10: Recursion fits lists well: handle the first element, call the function again on the rest, and stop at the empty list. `null` checks for the empty list.
loops.lesson.12: Without a base case, a recursive function calls itself again and again until the program stops with an error.
loops.card.2: `(loop for i from 1 to 5 collect i)`, also `sum`, `do`
loops.card.3: Recursion: base case first, then call with a smaller value
loops-1.explain: `i` takes the values 0, 1, 2 and 3. The text has no `~%`, so they print on one line.
loops-4.explain: `dolist` visits every element, but `when` prints only the odd ones.

loops-6.explain: The factorial multiplies: 4 times 3 times 2 times 1 is 24.

data.title: Local variables and data
data.summary: Use local variables with let, change values with setf, and store data in hash tables and structures.
data.lesson.0: `let` creates **local variables**. They exist only inside the body of the `let`. The first part is a list of pairs: a name and its value.
data.lesson.2: `let` creates all its variables at the same time, so one value cannot use another variable of the same `let`. `let*` creates them one after another, so later values can use earlier ones.
data.lesson.4: `setf` gives a variable a new value. `incf` adds 1 to a variable, or the number you give it.
data.lesson.7: A **hash table** stores values under keys. `(make-hash-table :test #'equal)` creates one. Words that start with a colon, like `:test`, are **keywords**; they name an argument. `:test #'equal` lets you use strings as keys. `(gethash key table)` reads a value, and `(setf (gethash key table) value)` stores one. A missing key gives `NIL`, or the default value you pass as a third argument. `incf` also works on `(gethash key table 0)`, which makes counting easy. `hash-table-count` counts the entries.
data.lesson.10: `defstruct` defines a new kind of record with named fields. `(defstruct point x y)` creates the function `make-point`, the readers `point-x` and `point-y`, and the test `point-p`. You give the field values with keywords, like `:x 3`. `setf` also changes a field.
data.lesson.12: A variable from `let` does not exist outside the `let`. Using it there stops the program with an error.
data.card.2: `(gethash key table)` read, `(setf (gethash key table) v)` store
